lessons.title: Sketching straight lines
lessons.summary: Use intercepts and gradient to sketch any line with a readable axis scale.
lessons.objective: Use intercepts and gradient to sketch any line with a readable axis scale.
lessons.before: Recall that a crossing point lies on the graph and the axis.
lessons.ideas:
Mark the y-intercept on the vertical axis.

Use both intercepts when they are different. If they coincide at the origin, find a separate point.

Rearrange to y = mx + c when possible to read gradient and intercept.
lessons.method:
Which coordinate is zero at the y-axis?

A line meets the vertical axis when x is zero. Substitute that value to find the crossing.

Which coordinate is zero at the x-axis?

Set the vertical coordinate to zero. Solve for the horizontal coordinate.

What does the gradient tell me about the line?

A positive gradient rises to the right and a negative gradient falls to the right. A gradient of zero gives a horizontal line.
mistakes: A y-intercept is a point with x-coordinate zero.
A line parallel to the horizontal axis may have no x-intercept.
A vertical line has equation x = a. Its gradient is undefined.

examples.title: Find where a line crosses the y-axis
examples.question: Find the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of \(y=-5x+7\).
examples.solution:
At the y-axis the x-coordinate is zero.

Substitute \(x=0\) into the line equation.

The answer is \(7\).

examples.title: Find where a line crosses the x-axis
examples.question: Find the x-intercept of \(y=6x+8\). Give its x-coordinate exactly.
examples.solution:
At the x-axis, y is zero.

Set \(6x+8=0\) and divide by the coefficient of x.

The answer is \(-\frac{4}{3}\).

examples.title: Read the gradient after rearranging
examples.question: Find the gradient of \(21x+3y=27\).
examples.solution:
Move the x term to the right. Then divide all terms by 3.

The line takes the form \(y=-7x+9\). The coefficient of x is the gradient.

The answer is \(-7\).

lessons.title: Sketching quadratics with roots and symmetry
lessons.summary: Identify the opening direction, root positions and line of symmetry before drawing the parabola.
lessons.objective: Identify the opening direction, root positions and line of symmetry before drawing the parabola.
lessons.before: Recall that a crossing point lies on the graph and the axis.
lessons.ideas:
The sign controls whether the curve cups up or arches down.

Find the mean of the two root values to locate the mirror line.

Write the y-intercept as a point and keep it separate from the x-intercepts.
lessons.method:
Does the parabola open up or down?

Read the sign of the squared term. A positive leading coefficient makes both ends rise.

Where is the vertical line of symmetry?

The parabola has a vertical mirror line. If it has two roots, they lie at equal horizontal distances from this mirror line.

Which crossing can I find without solving a quadratic?

At the y-axis, use x equal to zero. In the expanded form this leaves the constant. In the factorised form substitute into both brackets.
mistakes: The constant term identifies a vertical-axis crossing. It does not decide the opening direction.
A line of symmetry is a vertical line, not one of the roots.
Use two roots to mark crossings only when they are real.

examples.title: Choose the correct opening direction
examples.question: Sketch \(y=5(x+5)(x-7)\), showing the opening direction and both x-intercepts.
examples.solution:
The coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(5\).

Its sign determines the direction of opening.

The factor roots are \(-5\) and \(7\). Mark their x-intercepts before drawing the shape.

examples.title: Use symmetry between two roots
examples.question: The graph \(y=-6(x+6)(x-8)\) is symmetric about a vertical line. Give the x-value of that line exactly.
examples.solution:
The roots are \(-6\) and \(8\).

Find their midpoint: \(\frac{-6+8}{2}\).

The answer is \(1\).

examples.title: Find where a parabola meets the y-axis
examples.question: Find the y-coordinate where \(y=2(x+7)(x-9)\) meets the y-axis.
examples.solution:
Use x = 0 in the factorised form. The two factor values are \(7\) and \(-9\).

Multiply the two values by \(2\).

The answer is \(-126\).

lessons.title: Sketching a quadratic from its turning point (Extended)
lessons.summary: Complete the square to locate a minimum or maximum and use it to guide the sketch.
lessons.objective: Complete the square to locate a minimum or maximum and use it to guide the sketch.
lessons.before: Recall that a crossing point lies on the graph and the axis.
lessons.ideas:
Read the turning x-coordinate from the value that makes the bracket zero.

Mark the turning point and use the vertical line through it for symmetry.

A positive leading term gives a minimum, a negative leading term gives a maximum.
lessons.method:
Which x gives the turning point?

In completed-square form find the value of x where the whole bracket is zero. This is where the square makes no contribution.

Which y-value goes with that x?

When the squared bracket is zero, the other term gives the y-coordinate. Read the outside constant after completing the square.

Is this point a maximum or a minimum?

The square is non-negative. A positive multiplier raises all other outputs; a negative one lowers them.
mistakes: A negative sign inside the bracket can lead to a positive coordinate.
If a factor multiplies the bracket, keep track of it during every step of rearranging.
A parabola can have its turning point above, below or on the x-axis.

examples.title: Find the x-coordinate of the turning point
examples.question: Use completing the square to find the x-coordinate of the turning point of \(y=-5x^2+50x-119\).
examples.solution:
Take out the coefficient of \(x^2\) from the two x terms and complete the square.

The completed form is \(y=-5(x-5)^2+6\). The square is zero at the stated x-coordinate.

The answer is \(5\).

examples.title: Find a maximum or minimum value
examples.question: Use completing the square to find the minimum y-value of \(y=2x^2-24x+79\).
examples.solution:
Completing the square gives \(y=2(x-6)^2+7\).

At the turning point the squared term is zero. The constant outside the square gives the y-value.

The answer is \(7\).

examples.title: Choose the type of a turning point
examples.question: Does \(y=-3(x-7)^2+8\) have a minimum or a maximum? Explain your choice.
examples.solution:
The squared bracket is never negative. The multiplier is \(-3\).

The graph's turning value occurs when the square is zero, so the point is \((7,8)\).

lessons.title: Sketching cubic curves (Extended)
lessons.summary: Look at the cube term, intercepts and the possible changes in direction between roots.
lessons.objective: Look at the cube term, intercepts and the possible changes in direction between roots.
lessons.before: Recall that a crossing point lies on the graph and the axis.
lessons.ideas:
Use x equal to zero for the y-intercept. Use y equal to zero and a cube root to find the x-intercept.

For three distinct roots, the graph crosses three times and changes direction between successive crossings.

A positive leading term rises to the right; a negative leading term falls to the right.
lessons.method:
How does a translated cubic meet the axes?

Start from the basic increasing or decreasing cube curve. A constant added to it shifts every point vertically.

How do three factors give three crossings?

A product of three linear factors is zero when one factor is zero. Locate those x-values before sketching.

What decides the far ends of the graph?

Far from the origin, the cube term dominates the lower powers. The sign of its coefficient controls the direction.
mistakes: The graph of a positive cube has opposite end directions on the left and right.
If a factor occurs twice, the curve may touch the axis there. Mark repeated roots separately.
The sketch need not show exact turning point coordinates unless the question asks for them.

examples.title: Find the intercept of a translated cubic
examples.question: What is the y-intercept value for \(y=-5x^3+5\)?
examples.solution:
At the y-axis the x-value is zero.

The cube term vanishes, leaving \(5\).

The answer is \(5\).

examples.title: List every axis crossing of a cubic
examples.question: Give the complete set of x-intercepts of \(y=6x(x+6)(x-7)\), as a set of x-values.
examples.solution:
At each x-intercept, the product of the three factors is zero.

Set each factor to zero. The three x-values are \(-6, 0, 7\).

examples.title: Decide which way the cubic ends point
examples.question: As x increases far to the right, does \(y=-2x(x+7)(x-8)\) rise or fall? Explain your choice.
examples.solution:
The highest power is a cube with coefficient \(-2\).

For large positive x, every x factor is positive, so the sign of the multiplier controls the right end.

lessons.title: Sketching reciprocal curves (Extended)
lessons.summary: Locate an excluded x-value, two asymptotes and the correct side for each branch.
lessons.objective: Locate an excluded x-value, two asymptotes and the correct side for each branch.
lessons.before: Recall that a crossing point lies on the graph and the axis.
lessons.ideas:
The line x = 0 is vertical. The added constant gives the horizontal line approached.

A crossing of the x-axis is different from crossing the horizontal asymptote.

For a positive numerator, the right branch stays above the horizontal asymptote. A negative numerator swaps the branches.
lessons.method:
What lines does a reciprocal approach?

The graph is undefined at x equal to zero. On both sides, fractions with very large denominators get close to zero in size.

Can the curve cross the horizontal axis?

To locate an x-intercept set y to zero. Keep the condition that the denominator is non-zero while solving.

Which side of the asymptote is each branch on?

Compare y with the height of the horizontal asymptote. The sign of the fraction gives the side.
mistakes: Draw two separate branches. Do not connect the graph at its excluded input.
A line can be approached without being reached.
The branches can be both above or below the x-axis over part of a sketch after shifting.

examples.title: Find a horizontal asymptote
examples.question: Give the y-value of the horizontal asymptote of \(y=\frac{-5}{x}+6\).
examples.solution:
For large positive or negative x, the fraction tends to zero.

The constant \(6\) is the value approached.

The answer is \(6\).

examples.title: Find the zero of a shifted reciprocal
examples.question: Give the x-intercept of \(y=\frac{6}{x}+7\) as an exact x-coordinate.
examples.solution:
At an x-intercept use y = 0 and keep the condition that x is non-zero.

Multiply by x to obtain \(6+7x=0\). Solve and check the denominator.

The answer is \(-\frac{6}{7}\).

examples.title: Place the right-hand reciprocal branch
examples.question: For positive x, is \(y=\frac{-7}{x}+8\) above or below its horizontal asymptote? Explain your choice.
examples.solution:
The difference from \(y=8\) is \(\frac{-7}{x}\).

The denominator is positive on the right. The sign of the numerator tells you which side of the asymptote the branch lies on.

lessons.title: Sketching exponential curves (Extended)
lessons.summary: Use the base, vertical shift and value at x equal to zero to guide an exponential sketch.
lessons.objective: Use the base, vertical shift and value at x equal to zero to guide an exponential sketch.
lessons.before: Recall that a crossing point lies on the graph and the axis.
lessons.ideas:
The y-intercept is the outside coefficient plus the constant shift.

Draw the shifted horizontal asymptote with a dashed line.

Use the base first. A negative outside multiplier reverses the direction, and a vertical shift moves the whole curve.
lessons.method:
What happens at x equal to zero?

A positive base raised to zero is one. Multiply it by the outside coefficient, then add the shift.

Which horizontal line is approached?

At one end the exponential term tends to zero. The rest of the expression is the constant shift.

How can I tell whether it grows to the right?

For a positive multiplier, a base bigger than one increases and a base between zero and one decreases.
mistakes: The base to power zero is one, so the exponential term remains.
An exponential has no vertical asymptote in these forms.
A vertical shift alone does not change the direction of the curve.

examples.title: Find the y-intercept from the zero exponent
examples.question: Find the y-intercept value of \(y=5\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^x-7\).
examples.solution:
An exponential at x = 0 has a power equal to 1.

The y-intercept value is \(5-7\).

The answer is \(-2\).

examples.title: Find the shifted exponential asymptote
examples.question: Give the y-value of the horizontal asymptote of \(y=6\left(2\right)^x-8\).
examples.solution:
At one end, the exponential term tends to zero.

The graph approaches \(y=-8\), the vertical shift from the x-axis.

The answer is \(-8\).

examples.title: Recognise an increasing or decreasing exponential
examples.question: Does \(y=7\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^x-9\) increase or decrease to the right? Explain your choice.
examples.solution:
The base is \(\frac{1}{3}\) and the outside multiplier is positive.

A base above one gives growth. A base between zero and one gives decay.

1. Does \(y=-3(x-4)^2+176\) have a minimum or a maximum? Explain your choice.

    Show your working.

    [2]

  2. Use completing the square to find the maximum y-value of \(y=-3x^2+42x+41\).

    Show your working.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The squared bracket is never negative. The multiplier is \(-3\).

The graph's turning value occurs when the square is zero, so the point is \((4,176)\).

Answer: A maximum.

(b)

Completing the square gives \(y=-3(x-7)^2+188\).

At the turning point the squared term is zero. The constant outside the square gives the y-value.

The answer is \(188\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

With a negative multiplier, the square makes all other y-values smaller.

(b)

Keep the outside coefficient when completing the square.
